items.title: Elasticsearch Component for Home-Assistant
items.text:
Publish Home Assistant events to your Elasticsearch cluster!

Elasticsearch is a search and analytics engine for storing and exploring large amounts of data, and Kibana is its companion app for charts and dashboards. Sending your Home Assistant history there lets you keep it for as long as you choose, and analyze it across your whole home.

items.title: Features
items.text:
• Efficiently publishes Home-Assistant events to Elasticsearch using the Bulk API
  • Automatically sets up Datastreams using Time Series Data Streams ("TSDS") and Datastream Lifecycle Management ("DLM")
  • Supports Elastic's stack security features via optional username, password, and API keys
  • Selectively publish events based on labels, entities, devices, areas, or floors

items.title: Compatibility
items.text:
• Elasticsearch 8.14+ (Self, Cloud, or Serverless).
  • Elastic Common Schema version 1.0.0
  • Home Assistant Community Store
  • Home Assistant >= 2026.10

items.title: Older versions
items.text: Version 1.0.0 includes support for 7.11 to 8.13. No features or bugfixes will be backported to this version. Version 0.4.0 includes support for versions of Elasticsearch older than 7.11. No features or bugfixes will be backported to this version.

items.title: Gather Elasticsearch details
items.text:
You will need the following details to configure the Elasticsearch integration:

  1. The URL of your Elasticsearch instance
  2. Credentials to access the Elasticsearch instance (if required)
  3. The SSL certificate authority (CA) file, if you are using a custom CA not trusted by the host system

Use the URL of a supported Elasticsearch cluster. An Elasticsearch-compatible ingestion endpoint, such as VictoriaLogs' /insert/elasticsearch/, is not sufficient: this integration also requires Elasticsearch cluster metadata, security APIs, index templates, and data streams. Incompatible server metadata is reported as an unsupported server during setup.

Existing entries stop retrying setup when the server metadata is incompatible or a successful response is missing the X-Elastic-Product: Elasticsearch header. This includes a reverse proxy temporarily returning a success page while Elasticsearch starts. Once the endpoint is ready or its configuration is corrected, reload the integration to try again.

items.title: Credentials
items.text:
You must provide credentials if your Elasticsearch instance is secured. While we support authenticating via username/password, we recommend using API Keys for simplicity and compatibility with all versions of Elasticsearch.

Use the following command to create an API Key for the Home Assistant component.:

curlDev Tools 
ES_URL=https://localhost:9200 # (1)
ES_USER=elastic # (2)
ES_PASSWORD=changeme # (3)
curl "$ES_URL/_security/api_key" \
  -X POST \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -u "$ES_USER":"$ES_PASSWORD" \
  -d'
  {
    "name": "home_assistant_component",
    "role_descriptors": {
      "hass_writer": {
        "cluster": [
          "manage_index_templates",
          "monitor"
        ],
        "indices": [
          {
            "names": [
              "metrics-homeassistant.*"
            ],
            "privileges": [
              "manage",
              "index",
              "create_index",
              "create"
            ]
          }
        ]
      }
    }
  }
'
  1. Replace https://localhost:9200 with the URL of your Elasticsearch instance.
  2. Replace elastic with your Elasticsearch username.
  3. Replace changeme with your Elasticsearch password.
POST /_security/api_key
{
  "name": "home_assistant_component",
  "role_descriptors": {
    "hass_writer": {
      "cluster": [
        "manage_index_templates",
        "monitor"
      ],
      "indices": [
        {
          "names": [
            "metrics-homeassistant.*"
          ],
          "privileges": [
            "manage",
            "index",
            "create_index",
            "create"
          ]
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}

The API Key will be returned in the response. Save the encoded field for use in the configuration.

Read the Elasticsearch documentation for more information on creating API Keys.

items.title: Add the integration
items.text:
This component is configured interactively via Home Assistant's integration configuration page.

  1. Verify you have restarted Home Assistant after installing the component.
  2. From the Integrations configuration menu, add a new Elasticsearch integration.
  3. Provide the URL of your elasticsearch server in the format https://<host>:<port>. For example, https://localhost:9200.
  4. If your Elasticsearch instance is untrusted, you will be prompted to provide the path to the CA file or disable certificate verification.
  5. If your Elasticsearch instance is secured, you will be prompted to provide either a username and password or an API Key.
  6. Once the integration is setup, you may tweak all configuration options via the Configure button on the integrations page.

Each Elasticsearch cluster can only be added once, even when it can be reached through more than one URL.

items.title: Change connection settings
items.text:
To change the URL or TLS settings of an existing integration entry, open the entry's menu on the integrations page and select Reconfigure. Your credentials and configuration options are kept.

The form shows the entry's current settings:

  • URL to access the Elasticsearch Cluster - The address of your cluster, including the scheme and port.
  • Verify TLS certificate - Check that the server's certificate is signed by a trusted certificate authority.
  • Verify hostname matches server certificate - Check that the certificate was issued for the host in the URL.
  • Fully qualified path to custom certificate authority - Leave empty to use the system's trusted certificates.

The new settings are tested with the entry's saved credentials before they are saved. If the cluster rejects those credentials, you will be prompted for new ones, using the same authentication method.

The new URL must reach the same Elasticsearch cluster. To publish to a different cluster, add it as a new integration entry.

Note

An entry that has no saved TLS settings verifies the server's certificate and hostname. If an entry stops connecting after an update because its certificate can't be verified, use Reconfigure to provide a CA path or turn verification off.

items.title: Configuration options
items.text: Select Configure from the integration's homepage to configure the following settings.

items.title: Send events to Elasticsearch at this interval
items.text: The frequency at which events are published to Elasticsearch, in seconds. The default is 60.

items.title: Gather all entity states at this interval
items.text: The frequency at which all entity states are gathered, in seconds. The default is 60.

items.title: Choose what types of entity changes to listen for and publish
items.text:
There are two types of entity changes that can be published to Elasticsearch: - Track entities with state changes - Publish entities when their state changes - Track entities with attribute changes - Publish entities when their attributes change

Enabling both options will publish entities when either their state or attributes change.

items.title: Tags to apply to all published events
items.text: Tags are values that can be used to filter events in Elasticsearch. You can use this to add tags to all published events.

items.title: Toggle to only publish the set of targets below
items.text:
Pick floor, area, device, entity, or labels and only publish events from one of these targets. If you select multiple targets, events that match any of the targets will be published. If you select no targets, no events will be published.

An entity without an area of its own uses the area of its device, and belongs to the floor of that area.

Label targets match labels assigned directly to either the entity or its device. See Published fields for how labels, areas, and floors appear in Elasticsearch documents.

items.title: Toggle to exclude publishing the set of targets below
items.text: Pick floor, area, device, entity, or labels and exclude events from one of these targets. If you select multiple targets, events that match any of the targets will be excluded. If you also configure Toggle to only publish the set of targets below, the exclusion will be applied after the inclusion.

items.title: Custom certificate authority (CA)
items.text:
This component will use the system's default certificate authority (CA) bundle to verify the Elasticsearch server's certificate. If you need to use a custom CA, you can provide the path to the CA file in the integration configuration.

  1. Place the CA file somewhere within Home Assistant's configuration directory.
  2. Follow the steps above to add the integration.
  3. After providing connection details, the component will attempt to establish a connection to the Elasticsearch server. If the server's certificate is not signed by a known CA, you will be prompted for the CA file's path.
  4. Provide the path to the CA file and continue with the setup.

Note

You can choose to bypass certificate verification during setup, if you do not have the CA file available.

To change the CA path or the verification settings later, reconfigure the entry.

items.title: Advanced ingest configuration
items.text:
Note

This section describes advanced use cases. Most users will not need to customize their ingest configuration.

items.title: Defining your own Index Mappings, Settings, and Ingest Pipeline
items.text: You can customize the mappings, settings and define an ingest pipeline by creating a component template called metrics-homeassistant@custom

items.title: Custom Ingest Pipeline
items.text:
The following is an example on how to push your Home Assistant metrics into an ingest pipeline called metrics-homeassistant-pipeline:

Dev Toolscurl

Run these commands using Kibana's Dev Tools console:

PUT _ingest/pipeline/metrics-homeassistant-pipeline
{
    "description": "Pipeline for HomeAssistant dataset",
    "processors": [ ]
}

PUT _component_template/metrics-homeassistant@custom
{
    "template": {
        "mappings": {},
        "settings": {
            "index.default_pipeline": "metrics-homeassistant-pipeline"
        }
    }
}

ES_URL=https://localhost:9200 # (1)
ES_USER=elastic # (2)
ES_PASSWORD=changeme # (3)
curl -X PUT "$ES_URL/_ingest/pipeline/metrics-homeassistant-pipeline" \
    -u "$ES_USER":"$ES_PASSWORD" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d'
    {
        "description": "Pipeline for HomeAssistant dataset",
        "processors": [ ]
    }
    ' # (4)

curl -X PUT "$ES_URL/_component_template/metrics-homeassistant@custom" \
    -u "$ES_USER":"$ES_PASSWORD" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d'
    {
        "template": {
            "mappings": {},
            "settings": {
                "index.default_pipeline": "metrics-homeassistant-pipeline"
            }
        }
    }
    '
  1. Replace https://localhost:9200 with the URL of your Elasticsearch instance
  2. Replace elastic with your Elasticsearch username
  3. Replace changeme with your Elasticsearch password
  4. Add your ingest pipeline processors to the processors array

Component template changes apply when the datastream performs a rollover so the first time you modify the template you may need to manually initiate index/datastream rollover to start applying the pipeline.

items.title: Custom Attribute mappings
items.text:
Attributes are mapped as text with a .keyword subfield by default. To use an attribute in numeric aggregations, define a custom mapping. The following example maps hass.entity.attributes.temperature as a float:

Dev Toolscurl

Run these commands using Kibana's Dev Tools console:

PUT /_component_template/metrics-homeassistant@custom
{
    "template": {
        "mappings": {
            "properties": {
                "hass.entity.attributes": {
                    "type": "object",
                    "properties": {
                        "temperature": {
                            "type": "float",
                            "ignore_malformed": true
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

ES_URL=https://localhost:9200 # (1)
ES_USER=elastic # (2)
ES_PASSWORD=changeme # (3)

curl -X PUT "$ES_URL/_component_template/metrics-homeassistant@custom" \
    -u "$ES_USER":"$ES_PASSWORD" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d'
    {
        "template": {
            "mappings": {
                "properties": {
                    "hass.entity.attributes": {
                        "type": "object",
                        "properties": {
                            "temperature": {
                                "type": "float",
                                "ignore_malformed": true
                            }
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
    '
  1. Replace https://localhost:9200 with the URL of your Elasticsearch instance
  2. Replace elastic with your Elasticsearch username
  3. Replace changeme with your Elasticsearch password
  4. Modify the body of the component template to include desired mappings

items.title: HACS (recommended)
items.text:
This component is available in HACS (Home Assistant Community Store).

  1. Install HACS if you don't have it already
  2. Open HACS in Home Assistant
  3. Go to "Integrations" section
  4. Click button with "+" icon
  5. Search for "Elasticsearch"

items.title: Manual
items.text:
1. Download the latest release from the releases page
  2. Extract the contents of the zip file
  3. Copy the custom_components directory to your $HASS_CONFIG/custom_components directory, where $HASS_CONFIG is the location on your machine where Home-Assistant lives. Example: /home/pi/.homeassistant and /home/pi/.homeassistant/custom_components. You may have to create the custom_components directory yourself.

You must restart Home Assistant after installation.

Next: Configuration

items.title: Removing the integration
items.text:
1. From the Integrations configuration menu, select Elasticsearch, then delete each of its entries.
  2. If you installed with HACS, remove Elasticsearch from HACS. Otherwise, delete the custom_components/elasticsearch directory.
  3. Restart Home Assistant.

Home Assistant stops publishing at this point, but nothing is removed from Elasticsearch. Your existing data stays where it is, along with the following:

  • The metrics-homeassistant.* data streams, which hold your data
  • The metrics-homeassistant index template
  • Any API key or user you created for this integration

If you no longer need them, you can delete the data streams and then the index template, in that order, from Dev Tools in Kibana:

Warning

This permanently deletes all of the data published by Home Assistant.

DELETE _data_stream/metrics-homeassistant.*
DELETE _index_template/metrics-homeassistant

Then invalidate the API key, which you can do from Stack Management > API keys in Kibana.

items.title: Published fields
items.text:
Each published document contains an entity's state, its Home Assistant registry metadata, and details about how it was collected. Use these fields to filter documents in Discover and build visualizations in Lens. See Using Kibana to create a data view first.

Fields whose values are unavailable, null, or empty lists or objects are omitted. For example, an entity without a device has no hass.entity.device.* fields, and an entity without labels has no hass.entity.labels field.

items.title: Entity identity and metadata
items.text:
Field Type Description hass.entity.id Keyword Full entity ID, such as sensor.living_room_temperature. hass.entity.object.id Keyword Entity ID without its domain, such as living_room_temperature. hass.entity.domain Keyword Entity domain, such as sensor or climate. hass.entity.friendly_name Keyword Display name from the entity's state, falling back to its object ID with underscores replaced by spaces. Use this for a human-readable name in Kibana. hass.entity.name Keyword Name from the entity registry: the user-provided name, or the integration's original name. This can differ from the friendly name. hass.entity.platform Keyword Integration platform that provides the entity, such as esphome. hass.entity.device_class Keyword Entity's device class from the registry, preferring a user override to the original class, such as temperature. hass.entity.unit_of_measurement Keyword Unit recorded in the entity registry, such as °C or kWh. hass.entity.labels Keyword array IDs of labels assigned directly to the entity. hass.entity.device.id Keyword ID of the entity's device in the Home Assistant device registry. hass.entity.device.name Keyword Device's user-provided name, or its original name. hass.entity.device.labels Keyword array IDs of labels assigned directly to the device.

Label values are registry IDs, such as energy_monitoring, rather than display names such as Energy monitoring. Entity labels and device labels are published separately; neither list includes the other's labels or labels assigned to an area.

items.title: Areas, floors, and coordinates
items.text:
Field Type Description hass.entity.area.id Keyword ID of the area assigned directly to the entity. hass.entity.area.name Keyword Name of the area assigned directly to the entity. hass.entity.area.floor.id Keyword ID of the floor containing the entity's directly assigned area. hass.entity.area.floor.name Keyword Name of that floor. hass.entity.device.area.id Keyword ID of the area assigned to the device. hass.entity.device.area.name Keyword Name of the area assigned to the device. hass.entity.device.area.floor.id Keyword ID of the floor containing the device's area. hass.entity.device.area.floor.name Keyword Name of that floor. hass.entity.location Geo point Entity's coordinates as [longitude, latitude], when both state attributes are available.

The published entity area and floor describe only the entity's own area assignment. If the entity has no directly assigned area, those fields are omitted even when its device has an area. The device's area and floor remain available under hass.entity.device.area.*.

The publish target filters use the device's area and floor when the entity has no area of its own. This fallback determines which events are published; it does not copy device metadata into the entity's fields.

items.title: State values
items.text:
Field Type Description hass.entity.value Text Original state as a string, such as "72.5" or "on". Use its .keyword subfield for exact matching or grouping. hass.entity.valueas.float Float Numeric state, including whole numbers, such as 72.5 or 72.0. Use this for numeric charts and aggregations. hass.entity.valueas.boolean Boolean State converted to true or false. hass.entity.valueas.datetime Date Parsed date and time, such as 2024-04-10T16:23:25.878000+00:00. hass.entity.valueas.date Date Date portion of a parsed datetime, such as 2024-04-10. hass.entity.valueas.time Date Time portion of a parsed datetime, such as 16:23:25.878000. hass.entity.valueas.string Text State when no boolean, numeric, or datetime conversion succeeds. Also has a .keyword subfield.

The original value is always published. The integration attempts conversions in this order: boolean, number, then datetime. The first successful conversion determines which valueas.* fields appear. A datetime conversion produces all three of datetime, date, and time; otherwise, only one converted field is published.

Boolean conversion recognizes true, on, locked, above_horizon, open, and home as true; false, off, unlocked, unknown, below_horizon, closed, and not_home as false. Other states are tried as numbers and datetimes before falling back to a string.

items.title: State attributes
items.text:
Other supported state attributes appear under hass.entity.attributes.*. Attribute names are normalized to lowercase ASCII, with punctuation and whitespace replaced by underscores. For example, Fan Speed becomes hass.entity.attributes.fan_speed. If two names normalize to the same key, the later attribute replaces the earlier one.

The following attributes are excluded from this object:

State attribute Published representation friendly_name hass.entity.friendly_name device_class hass.entity.device_class, sourced from the entity registry unit_of_measurement hass.entity.unit_of_measurement, sourced from the entity registry entity_picture, icon, state_class Omitted.

When updating older dashboards, use hass.entity.friendly_name instead of hass.entity.attributes.friendly_name. Device class and unit of measurement also have dedicated fields rather than copies under attributes.

Attributes are dynamically mapped as text with a .keyword subfield by default. Numeric state attributes therefore need a custom attribute mapping if you want numeric aggregations. Dictionary-valued attributes are serialized as JSON strings; sets are converted to sorted lists. Attributes with unsupported value types or non-string or blank keys are skipped.

Outside the attributes object, extra fields without an explicit mapping are kept in the stored document but are not indexed for searching or aggregations. Add a custom mapping if you need to query those fields.

items.title: Event, data stream, and host details
items.text:
Field Type Description @timestamp Date with nanosecond precision Time the state change was collected, or the time of the polling pass, rather than the time the batch reached Elasticsearch. event.action Keyword Collection reason: Polling, State change, or Attribute change. event.kind Keyword Always event. event.type Keyword info for polling; change for state or attribute changes. data_stream.type Constant keyword Always metrics. data_stream.dataset Constant keyword homeassistant.<domain>, such as homeassistant.sensor. data_stream.namespace Constant keyword Always default. tags Keyword array Tags configured for all events. These are separate from Home Assistant labels. agent.version Keyword Home Assistant version. host.architecture Keyword Architecture reported by Home Assistant. host.os.name Keyword Operating system name reported by Home Assistant. host.hostname Keyword Supervisor-reported hostname when available, otherwise the runtime's hostname. host.location Geo point Home Assistant's configured home coordinates as [longitude, latitude].

Host details and tags are gathered when the integration starts. Data stream fields determine the destination, such as metrics-homeassistant.sensor-default.

items.title: Example document
items.text:
This example shows a temperature entity assigned directly to the Living Room area, with an associated device in the same area. The area belongs to the Ground Floor. Host details are left out for brevity. Documents use dotted field names:

{
  "@timestamp": "2026-11-06T18:00:00+00:00",
  "event.action": "State change",
  "event.kind": "event",
  "event.type": "change",
  "data_stream.type": "metrics",
  "data_stream.dataset": "homeassistant.sensor",
  "data_stream.namespace": "default",
  "hass.entity.id": "sensor.living_room_temperature",
  "hass.entity.object.id": "living_room_temperature",
  "hass.entity.domain": "sensor",
  "hass.entity.friendly_name": "Living Room Temperature",
  "hass.entity.name": "Temperature",
  "hass.entity.platform": "esphome",
  "hass.entity.device_class": "temperature",
  "hass.entity.unit_of_measurement": "°C",
  "hass.entity.labels": ["indoor"],
  "hass.entity.area.id": "living_room",
  "hass.entity.area.name": "Living Room",
  "hass.entity.area.floor.id": "ground_floor",
  "hass.entity.area.floor.name": "Ground Floor",
  "hass.entity.device.id": "abc123",
  "hass.entity.device.name": "Living Room Sensor",
  "hass.entity.device.labels": ["environment"],
  "hass.entity.device.area.id": "living_room",
  "hass.entity.device.area.name": "Living Room",
  "hass.entity.device.area.floor.id": "ground_floor",
  "hass.entity.device.area.floor.name": "Ground Floor",
  "hass.entity.attributes.battery_level": 95,
  "hass.entity.value": "21.5",
  "hass.entity.valueas.float": 21.5,
  "tags": ["home"]
}

items.title: Filter by floor or label in Kibana
items.text:
Use these examples in Discover's KQL search bar, replacing IDs with values from your documents.

To find entities on the Ground Floor, using the entity's own floor when assigned and otherwise the device's floor:

hass.entity.area.floor.id: "ground_floor" or
(not hass.entity.area.id: * and hass.entity.device.area.floor.id: "ground_floor")

To find entities labeled indoor either directly or through their device:

hass.entity.labels: "indoor" or hass.entity.device.labels: "indoor"

items.title: Using Kibana
items.text: The integration will put data into Elasticsearch under the metrics-homeassistant.* data stream. To explore your data, create visualizations, or dashboards in Kibana you first need to create a Data View.

items.title: Create a data view
Exploring Home Assistant data in Kibana
items.text:
Once you have created a Data View, you can start exploring your Home Assistant data in Kibana using Discover:

  1. In Kibana select Discover
  2. Select the Home Assistant Metrics Data View at the top left
  3. You can now see all the Home Assistant data that has been published to Elasticsearch
  4. You can filter the data using the filter bar at the top
  5. You can pull specific fields into the document table at the bottom by clicking on the + icon next to a field
  6. You can change the time range of the data you are viewing using the time picker in the top right

items.title: Viewing Home Assistant data in Kibana
items.text:
When creating new visualizations you may find the following fields useful. See Published fields for the full reference, including device names, labels, areas, floors, and attribute handling.

Field Description @timestamp The timestamp of the event (ex. Apr 10, 2024 @ 16:23:25.878) hass.entity.friendly_name The display name of the entity in Home Assistant (ex. Living Room EcoBee Temperature) hass.entity.device.name The name of the entity's device in Home Assistant (ex. Living Room EcoBee) hass.entity.device.area.name The area of the device in Home Assistant (ex. Living Room) hass.entity.id The entity id of the entity in Home Assistant (ex. sensor.living_room_ecobee_temperature) hass.entity.value The state of the entity in Home Assistant (ex. 72.5), as a string-typed value hass.entity.valueas.float The state of the entity in Home Assistant (ex. 72.5), as a float-typed value hass.entity.valueas.boolean The state of the entity in Home Assistant (ex. true), as a boolean-typed value hass.entity.valueas.date The state of the entity in Home Assistant (ex. 2024-04-10), as a date-typed value hass.entity.valueas.datetime The state of the entity in Home Assistant (ex. 2024-04-10T16:23:25.878), as a datetime-typed value hass.entity.valueas.time The state of the entity in Home Assistant (ex. 16:23:25.878), as a time-typed value

To build a visualization that shows the temperature of a specific entity over time, you can use the following steps:

  1. In Kibana select Visualizations and create a new Lens visualization
  2. Select Home Assistant Metrics
  3. For the Horizontal axis select @timestamp
  4. For the Vertical axis select hass.entity.valueas.float
  5. In the filter bar at the top, add a filter for hass.entity.id and set the value to the entity id of the entity you want to visualize (ex. sensor.living_room_ecobee_temperature) or hass.entity.friendly_name and set the value to the friendly name of the entity you want to visualize (ex. Living Room EcoBee Temperature)

items.title: Additional examples
items.text:
Some usage examples inspired by real users:

  • Utilizing a Raspberry Pi in kiosk mode with a 15" display, the homeassistant-elasticsearch integration enables the creation of rotating fullscreen Elasticsearch Canvas. Those canvas displays metrics collected from various Home Assistant integrations, offering visually dynamic and informative dashboards for monitoring smart home data.
  • To address temperature maintenance issues in refrigerators and freezers, temperature sensors in each appliance report data to Home Assistant, which is then published to Elasticsearch. Kibana's alerting framework is employed to set up rules that notify the user if temperatures deviate unfavorably for an extended period. The Elastic rule engine and aggregations simplify the monitoring process for this specific use case.
  • Monitoring the humidity and temperature in a snake enclosure/habitat for a user's daughter, the integration facilitates the use of Elastic's Alerting framework. This choice is motivated by the framework's suitability for the monitoring requirements, providing a more intuitive solution compared to Home Assistant automations.
  • The integration allows users to maintain a smaller subset of data, focusing on individual stats of interest, for an extended period. This capability contrasts with the limited retention achievable with Home Assistant and databases like MariaDB/MySQL. This extended data retention facilitates very long-term trend analysis, such as for weather data, enabling users to glean insights over an extended timeframe.
